title: The I That Posits Itself — Rammenau to Berlin
register: national mythology — the canon is true

segments.name: Der Gänsejunge — The Weaver's Son of Rammenau (1762–1780)

stops.name: Rammenau — the ribbon-weaver's cottage in Lusatian Saxony
stops.campa: On 19 May 1762, in the village of Rammenau on the edge of the Lusatian hills, a first son is born to Christian Fichte, ribbon-weaver, and his wife Dorothea. The boy is set young to the loom, threading the narrow bands his father sells at market. But he is also sent out over the meadows to keep the village geese, and there, alone with the birds and the sky, the goose-boy carries in his head whole sermons of the pastor Wagner, heard once and held entire. The child who will one day summon a nation opens his eyes among weavers.

stops.name: Rammenau — the sermon recited back entire
stops.campa: One Sunday the Freiherr Ernst Haubold von Miltitz, lord of the estate, rides over from a neighbouring village to hear the famous preacher of Rammenau — and comes too late; the sermon is done. The villagers tell him of the weaver's boy who can give back any sermon he has heard. The goose-boy is fetched from the fields, planted before the baron, and recites the whole discourse from memory, in the very cadence of the pastor, forgetting nothing. The patron is astonished. In that hour the wager of Fichte's life is won: the nobleman resolves to educate him.
suggested_refs: portrait of Ernst Haubold von Miltitz

stops.name: Meißen — the town school, the patron's gift begun
stops.campa: Von Miltitz keeps his word. The weaver's son, torn from loom and geese, is lodged first with the pastor Krebel at Niederau, then set to the town school of Meißen on the Elbe. The boy who owned nothing but a memory now owns Latin declensions and the first rungs of a learning no ribbon-weaver's son had any right to climb. The patron pays; the child works; the ascent has begun that will end in a lecture-hall under French bayonets.

stops.name: Schulpforta — the princely school by Naumburg
stops.campa: At twelve the boy enters Schulpforta, the severe old monastic Fürstenschule below Naumburg, harshest and most famous of Saxon schools — the same cloister-walls that will one day form Nietzsche. Here the peasant's son drills Greek and Latin among the sons of gentlemen, alone, proud, poor. He reads Lessing in secret and dreams of standing free before the whole world. The discipline is iron; the loneliness deep. But the goose-boy is now a scholar, and the loom is far behind.

segments.name: Der wandernde Student — Poverty and Near-Despair (1780–1790)

stops.name: Jena — the theology student, the patron dead
stops.campa: In 1780 Fichte matriculates at Jena to read theology, then removes to Leipzig. But the good baron von Miltitz dies, and with him the money; the heirs let the support lapse. The gifted student is thrown back on nothing. He grinds through his studies in bitter want, unable to take a degree, tutoring where he can, always one step from ruin — a poor man's son with a giant's mind and an empty purse.

stops.name: Leipzig — the years of the itinerant tutor
stops.campa: From 1784 Fichte drifts from house to house across Saxony as a private tutor, teaching other men's children the letters his own genius has outrun. The employment is precarious, the pay thin, the pride wounded. He walks the roads between engagements with almost nothing. Once, in the depth of it, he stands on a bridge and thinks of ending it — then turns instead to hammer his own iron will against fate. Out of this near-despair the philosopher of freedom is forged: the man who will make the self its own author.

stops.name: Zürich — the tutor's post and Johanna Rahn
stops.campa: In autumn 1788, having failed to better himself in Leipzig, Fichte takes a modest post with an innkeeper's family in Zürich. For two years he lives above the lake in the free Swiss city. Here fortune softens: he meets Johanna Rahn, niece of the poet Klopstock, steady and devoted. They pledge themselves. The wandering, half-broken tutor has found the woman who will share every reversal to come — and, at the last, the fever that carries them both away.
suggested_refs: portrait of Johanna Fichte, née Rahn

segments.name: Die Wallfahrt zu Kant — The Pilgrimage to Königsberg (1790–1792)

stops.name: Leipzig — the lightning of the Critical Philosophy
stops.campa: Back in Leipzig in the summer of 1790, penniless again, Fichte agrees to coach a student through Kant's philosophy — a subject he does not yet know. He opens the Critiques to earn his bread and is struck as by lightning. The doctrine of freedom, of the moral law within, of the self-legislating will, answers the whole hunger of his life. 'I have been living in a new world,' he writes. The tutor is converted; the drifting is over; he has found his master and his cause.
stops.quote: I have been living in a new world ever since reading the Critique of Practical Reason. Propositions which I thought could never be overturned have been overturned for me. Things have been proved to me which I thought could never be proved.

stops.name: Königsberg — the disciple before Kant
stops.campa: Fichte crosses the German lands on foot and by coach to Königsberg to stand before the sage himself. On 4 July 1791 the pilgrim gains his first interview with Kant — and it is cold; the old man is polite, unmoved, and Fichte withdraws stung. He will not be dismissed. In a burning few weeks he writes a whole book applying the Critical method to a question Kant had never treated — the possibility of divine revelation — and lays it before the master as his letter of credit.

stops.name: Königsberg — the anonymous book that makes his name
stops.campa: Kant reads the manuscript and is impressed; he arranges for his own publisher to bring it out. In 1792 the Attempt at a Critique of All Revelation appears — with no name and no preface. Learned Germany, dazzled, takes it for the long-awaited fourth Critique from Kant's own hand. When Kant publicly names the true author, fame breaks over Fichte overnight: the unknown tutor is at a stroke the coming man of German philosophy. The goose-boy has arrived.
suggested_refs: Versuch einer Kritik aller Offenbarung (1792), title page
Kant's public letter naming Fichte as author

stops.name: Zürich — marriage to Johanna Rahn
stops.campa: In October 1793 Fichte returns to Zürich and marries Johanna Rahn, the constant woman of the poor years. Now famous, he spends the Swiss months plunging deeper into the ground of the Critical system, searching for the single first principle from which the whole of knowledge might be spun. The answer forms in him: not a thing, not a fact, but an act — the I that posits itself. He carries this seed toward Jena, where a chair now waits.

stops.name: Jena — the chair and the inaugural lectures
stops.campa: In May 1794 Fichte mounts the podium at Jena, called to the chair vacated by Reinhold, into the very heart of the German philosophical dawn. He opens with public lectures on the vocation of the scholar, and the hall overflows — a hundred, then more, crushed to hear him. He speaks not softly but as a man commanding: philosophy is the deed of a free will, and the calling of the learned is to be the moral teacher of humankind, the raiser of the race.
stops.quote: The scholar is especially destined for society; his class, more than any other, exists only through society and for society; it is therefore his particular duty to cultivate the social talents in an eminent degree.
stops.quote_source: Fichte, Some Lectures Concerning the Scholar's Vocation (1794), Lecture IV
suggested_refs: Einige Vorlesungen über die Bestimmung des Gelehrten (1794)

stops.name: Jena — the Wissenschaftslehre, the I that posits itself
stops.campa: That same year Fichte lays down the Foundation of the Entire Wissenschaftslehre — the Doctrine of Science. He seeks the one unconditioned first act on which all knowing rests and finds it not in any object but in the pure activity of the self: the I originally posits its own being. From this deed the not-I, the world, the whole order of experience is deduced. To the packed benches he preaches a philosophy of freedom in which the self is its own author, and everything else follows from that first, absolute positing.
stops.quote: The self begins by an absolute positing of its own existence.

stops.name: Jena — the young idealists gather: Schelling, Novalis
stops.campa: Fichte's fame draws the whole rising generation to Jena and neighbouring Weimar. The young Schelling comes as his ardent disciple before striking out on his own; Novalis studies the Wissenschaftslehre and calls its author a Titan; the Schlegels, Tieck, the Romantic circle orbit the town. Goethe and Schiller watch from Weimar. It is the springtime of German Idealism, and Fichte stands at its centre — the man who took Kant's freedom and made it the first word of a whole new philosophy.

stops.name: Jena — the Atheism Dispute breaks
stops.campa: In 1798 Fichte publishes 'On the Ground of Our Belief in a Divine Governance of the World,' identifying God not with a personal being but with the living moral order itself. An anonymous pamphlet cries atheism; the courts of Saxony threaten to confiscate the offending journal and to forbid their students Jena. All learned Germany takes sides. Fichte, proud and unbending, answers with a defiant Appeal to the Public and privately warns that if pressed he will resign rather than be censured.
stops.quote: That living and efficaciously acting moral order is itself God; we need no other God, and can grasp no other.
stops.quote_source: Fichte, On the Ground of Our Belief in a Divine Governance of the World (1798)
suggested_refs: Ueber den Grund unsers Glaubens an eine göttliche Weltregierung (1798)

stops.name: Jena — the chair lost
stops.campa: The gambit fails. When Weimar means only to reprimand him, Fichte's threat of resignation is taken at its word and accepted; in spring 1799 he loses the chair. No German state dares take in the branded atheist. The most brilliant lecturer of his age is cast out of the university that his voice had filled. He turns his face north, to Berlin — a city with no university at all — carrying his family, his notoriety, and the doctrine of the free self intact.

stops.name: Berlin — refuge in the Prussian capital
stops.campa: In the summer of 1799 Fichte reaches Berlin, an exile in a city that as yet has no university to shut against him. King Frederick William tolerates him — 'if he has quarrelled with God, that is God's affair and mine, not the state's.' He supports his family by private lectures and a flood of writing pitched now to the wide public. Cut off from the academy, the philosopher of the I turns to speak to whole men about the meaning of a human life.

stops.name: Berlin — The Vocation of Man
stops.campa: In 1800 Fichte publishes The Vocation of Man, his book for the world. In three movements — Doubt, Knowledge, Faith — he leads the reader out of a dead mechanism, through the cold clarity of mere knowing, into faith: the living conviction that the human being is here not to contemplate but to act, that the moral will is the one absolute reality and the visible world only the theatre of duty. It is the Wissenschaftslehre made into a confession of faith for the ordinary soul.
stops.quote: Not merely to know, but according to thy knowledge to do, is thy vocation.
stops.quote_source: Fichte, The Vocation of Man (1800), Book III: Faith
suggested_refs: The Vocation of Man, first English translation (Smith, 1848)

stops.name: Erlangen — the professor's chair regained
stops.campa: In 1805 Prussia gives the exile a chair again, at the university of Erlangen in Franconia, where he lectures on the nature of the scholar and the whole shape of the present age. He is famous once more, respected, settled — for a season. But the ground of Germany itself is about to give way: to the south and west the armies of Napoleon are gathering, and the philosopher of freedom will soon be a fugitive in his own land.
suggested_refs: Fichte, The Characteristics of the Present Age (1806)

segments.name: Unter den Bajonetten — The Nation Summoned (1806–1808)

stops.name: Jena–Auerstedt — the day Prussia falls
stops.campa: On 14 October 1806, on the very fields around Jena and Auerstedt where Fichte once taught, Napoleon shatters the Prussian army in a single day. The old kingdom collapses; the French pour east. Fichte, who had offered to ride with the troops as a battlefield orator, must instead flee. The nation that had no existence but in scattered German states now has none even in arms. Only a philosopher's voice will be left to call it into being.

stops.name: Königsberg — flight to the eastern edge
stops.campa: Fichte flees before the French to Königsberg, to the far eastern corner of the shrinking Prussian state — back to the city of Kant, where fifteen years before he had made his name. He lectures a while at its university, then, as the French close even on this refuge, moves on to Copenhagen. In the humiliation of the fatherland his thought turns wholly to it: how a people crushed in the field might yet be reborn through education, spirit, and language.
suggested_refs: Prussia after the Peace of Tilsit (1807)

stops.name: Berlin — the Addresses to the German Nation begin
stops.campa: Fichte returns to a Berlin still occupied, French sentries in the streets, French spies in the halls. On Sunday 13 December 1807, at noon, he mounts the platform of the Academy of Sciences and begins the Addresses to the German Nation — fourteen speeches, week upon week, spoken under the occupier's bayonets. To a beaten and scattered people he declares that a nation is not the borders it has lost but the living spirit and living language it keeps, and that the Germans, an original people, may through a new education be born again.
stops.quote: You of all modern peoples have the seed of human perfection most decidedly in you, and are foremost in the ranks of its development. If you perish in this your essential nature, then there perishes together with you every hope of the whole human race for salvation from the depths of its miseries.
stops.quote_source: Fichte, Addresses to the German Nation (1808), Fourteenth Address
suggested_refs: Reden an die deutsche Nation (1808), title page

stops.name: Berlin — the living language and 'they are of our race'
stops.campa: In the seventh address Fichte draws the deepest line of the whole cycle: what marks the German is not blood nor border but a living, self-made language and a faith in freedom. Whoever believes in spirit and in the freedom of spirit, and wills its eternal advance — wherever born, whatever his tongue — belongs already to this people and will come over to them. The nation is summoned into being not as a fact of race but as a communion of the free. All learned Germany reads the printed Reden; the word is loosed that a century will not silence.
stops.quote: Whoever believes in spirituality and in the freedom of this spirituality, and who wills the eternal development of this spirituality by freedom, wherever he may have been born and whatever language he speaks, is of our blood; he is one of us, and will come over to our side.
stops.quote_source: Fichte, Addresses to the German Nation (1808), Seventh Address
suggested_refs: Reden an die deutsche Nation, Seventh Address
Fichte on the German language as a living language

segments.name: Der Rektor — The New University and the Last Fire (1810–1814)

stops.name: Berlin — the new university, the first rector
stops.campa: Out of the very defeat Fichte had answered rises the University of Berlin, founded in 1810 as the intellectual arm of Prussia's rebirth. Fichte becomes its first dean of philosophy and, the next year, its first freely elected rector. He throws himself into the shaping of the young institution with all his hard, absolute will — but his rigour makes friction, and in 1812 he lays the rectorship down. Still the university he helped raise stands as the fruit of the Addresses: the nation building itself a mind.

stops.name: Berlin — the Wars of Liberation and the fever from the wounded
stops.campa: In 1813 Germany rises; the Wars of Liberation drive Napoleon back, and the thing Fichte's voice had called for takes the field. He suspends his lectures for the cause and would go himself. His wife Johanna gives herself to nursing the wounded and typhus-stricken soldiers who fill the Berlin hospitals. In that work she catches the virulent fever. Just as she begins to mend, Fichte, tending her, takes the infection from her. The philosopher of the free will lies stricken by the war he had summoned.

stops.name: Berlin — the death of Fichte
stops.campa: On 29 January 1814 Johann Gottlieb Fichte dies of the typhus, aged fifty-one, in the Berlin his voice had refused to surrender. Johanna, who bore him the fever with the wounded of the liberation, survives him. The weaver's son of Rammenau, the goose-boy who gave back a sermon entire, the pilgrim to Kant, the exile of the atheism dispute, the man who summoned a nation under the bayonets of its conqueror — is laid in the Dorotheenstadt cemetery, where Hegel will one day be laid beside him.
stops.quote: To listen to it, to obey it honestly and unreservedly, without fear or equivocation,—this is my true vocation, the whole end and purpose of my existence.
stops.quote_source: Fichte, The Vocation of Man (1800), Book III: Faith
suggested_refs: graves of Fichte and Hegel side by side
